(1) The design reason for the truncation level (book p. 151, PDF p. 159): c_n is taken just large enough that the truncated and original sums agree with probability tending to one, and kept as low as possible so that the truncated variance is as small as possible. (2) The Remark that follows (book p. 152, PDF p. 160): if the tail x^{-2} is replaced by x^{-alpha}, 0 < alpha < 2, then S_n/n^{1/alpha} converges to a limit that is not normal (developed in the source's Section 3.6). components.gap: The Remarks after Theorem 3.4.17 (book p. 157, PDF p. 165) are only partly supplied. Present: the bound holds for all n and x and is trivial for n <= 9 because rho >= sigma^3, and the fair-sign obstruction to a rate faster than n^{-1/2} (annex lines 318-323 and 438-448). Missing: (1) the historical claim that 3 is not the best constant, with van Beek (1972) obtaining 0.8; (2) Feller's assessment, quoted by the source, of how good a bound the streamlined method gives; (3) the claim that the third-moment hypothesis is needed to get the rate n^{-1/2}; (4) Heyde's (1967) theorem: for 0 < delta < 1, sum over n of n^{-1+delta/2} sup_x |F_n(x) - N(x)| is finite if and only if E|X|^{2+delta} < infinity; (5) the pointer to Hall (1982) for more on rates. The boundary (body lines 555-557) only says that the Heyde rate equivalence remains separate; it states none of these.
